So there are so many great SaaS M&A stories out there, and I thought this one was particularly interesting — because we didn’t know what happened to Brex after Covid hit.
Brex was founded just before Covid hit in late 2019/early 2020, which put them right on the cusp of an epic crash. They were doing well, but they weren’t yet cash-flow positive.
And then … everything changed.  Everyone went remote, and card spend went way up.  Brex saw usage grow “threefold” in early 2020 (E6), and by June it had already doubled again (E7). It’s now worth a stunning $12 Billion (!) (E8).
They also added invoicing to their core offering during that time period (E9)

But even with all these incredible metrics, the bottom line is tough.  They weren’t profitable, and investors wanted to see more.
Fast forward to today, Brex is being acquired by Capital One for $5.15 Billion. That’s likely less than half of where it’s valued privately today, but still a very good outcome!
Why? Well, maybe the math is simple:
Capital One isn’t paying too much here, if they can turn it around.  You don’t need to pay full-up private valuation multiples when you acquire something and think you can improve it.  At least, not often.
In any event, kudos to Brex for building such a strong business!  A true rocketship.
Here’s wishing the team all the best moving forward!!

traces.answer: There are so many ways to fail hiring your first VP of Sales. One of my top mistakes was taking too long. I waited until we had just closed our Series B round before making the hire. Mistake. Another big one is hiring someone you’d personally buy from — if they aren't a true stretch VP of Sales candidate. They often don’t know how to manage people under them. Or scale processes. But probably the biggest mistake most founders make is hiring a “VP” of Sales that isn’t really a real manager, i.e., doesn’t have anyone reporting to her/him. At all. It’s easy for this to happen when times are tougher than planned. And there’s a lot of competition out there now. When things get harder, folks will settle on a new VP of Sales that … well, does some parts OK. They’ll close a few deals themselves. Maybe even grow revenue a bit. But can’t build anything under them. Can’t recruit any great reps to join their team. This is especially common today when startups are looking for magic fixes to boost growth quickly. Instead, they end up with someone that doesn’t really help much overall. So what are the best practices here? If you’re going to hire a VP of Sales without an experienced background (i.e., hasn’t been a real manager of 18+ people), then try to find someone that knows recruiting cold, that knows how to train, that knows how to scale processes, that knows how to take your product and get customers excited about buying it. Not sure she/he can do it

traces.answer:
So I've been lucky enough over the years to meet so many incredible VPs of Sales. And you know what? Incredibly successful ones just plain hire faster than less experienced ones. They go out there and they recruit more people on their own. Now when this doesn't happen, it can be tough to understand why. But let me give you some learnings:

First, if your VP of Sales isn't bringing in any reps themselves, he probably can't really sell himself. This is very common. A lot of folks that end up being VPs of Sales have never sold before. So, if they aren't recruiting anyone, well... they probably don't really know how to sell either. At least, not well enough. Maybe we need someone different here. Second, a mediocre VP of Sales will often claim she does recruit, but her recruits don't work out. Usually, for the same reasons his rep did. Third, a mediocre VP of Sales won't make any progress anyway. It's hard to see progress sometimes because it takes time. So the best thing you can do is find someone whose best people also perform well. And then trust him to scale. He'll get there. Just wait. Fourth, an amazing VP of Sales will always recruit ahead of where the company is today. This is perhaps the most important insight. If a truly great VP of Sales joins you -- she already knows what she needs for next quarter. She may even already have half the team recruited by Day One. Why? Because a truly great VP of Sales knows exactly what she wants to hit for the year, and she already knows the team needed to do that.

And those two things are what happens if this new VP of Sales doesn't perform well. And secondly, how many reps under him or her should they bring into the company. So let me just tell you my learnings here. First, if you don't have confidence in your first VP of Sales after you hire 'em, most likely you'll never trust 'em. Now some of you will disagree, some of you think maybe you can push through six months without trusting someone, but we all know that you're right. If you don't trust someone, they won't work out. They're going to fail. And so then the question is, can you give them enough time? Is it too early to criticize them? Do you need to support them longer than normal? Well, let me share an experience I had recently. It was one of our best investments ever. We invested in a company called Algolia. Today, they're at almost $100 million in revenue. Incredibly successful, public company, beautiful product, amazing business model. And they did something very similar to us. They hired a VP of Sales. He came from another company. We were excited to see how he would do. He started off strong for three or four months. Then it went downhill quickly. His performance was way below plan. There wasn't any improvement in his numbers. And as soon as he got there, he said he needed to bring in his own people. We didn't want him to.

So we've had some interesting discussions with folks like Clay and others who are doing AI, and one thing I want to take away today is what does it mean for you guys in your product to deliver personalization with AI?
Is it something that has to happen or should just kind of naturally occur?
I know a lot of people don't really believe there's any reason to personalize anything anymore because of AI.
But actually, I think that's wrong.
Because if you're selling to multiple stakeholders in an enterprise, you'll need to do all the things that you used to have to do before which is segment them and tailor your pitch so that they hear how your solution solves their problems.
And that's even more important now than ever.
There was a piece of software that I use called Salesloft.
It's CRM plus outreach.
They came out with an agent.
It's great, by the way.
One of the best ones I've seen.
But when they launched, it didn't work well.
The first version of the agent couldn't handle the nuances of different customers.
So then it went into production and I could see exactly what emails were being sent, right down to the last word.
So I tried it myself.
This email did go through, but the next day another email went through, and then no emails went through after that.
Well, why would that be?
Why would two emails go through and then stop?
Because the context changed between those two emails.
Those two emails were about two different prospects.
One was ready to buy and one wasn't ready to buy yet.
That's where the old world segmentation still matters.
Even though the agents are getting better, they aren't perfect yet.
But let me tell you what is amazing with these new tools.
When I saw that my account executive didn't get credit for the deal that closed, I immediately reached out to her via text message.
